introduction_section.heading: What is Engineering-Led
content: Engineering-led code architecture diagramming is the process of converting complex software structures into clear visual documentation. It can include class diagrams, dependency graphs, database schemas, API flows, routing maps, module boundaries, infrastructure diagrams, and frontend component structures.

At Devisgon, we create diagrams that are practical for real engineering work, not decorative illustrations. Our approach helps teams understand how code, databases, services, APIs, packages, routes, and components connect so they can reduce confusion, improve onboarding, identify risks, and plan refactoring with better visibility.
introduction_section.highlight_quote: “Clear architecture diagrams turn complex codebases into understandable systems, faster onboarding, and safer engineering decisions.”

faq_section.title: Code Architecture Diagram Questions and Answers
faq_section.subtitle: Detailed answers for founders, CTOs, technical leads, and engineering teams documenting software systems

questions.question: What are code architecture diagrams?
questions.answer: Code architecture diagrams are visual documents that show how software systems are structured. They can map modules, classes, APIs, databases, frontend routes, services, dependencies, and workflows. These diagrams help developers and stakeholders understand how the system works without reading every file manually.

questions.question: What types of diagrams can Devisgon create?
questions.answer: Devisgon can create UML class diagrams, ERDs, API flow diagrams, sequence diagrams, dependency graphs, component maps, routing diagrams, workflow diagrams, and high-level system architecture diagrams. The right diagram type depends on your codebase, team needs, and documentation goals.

questions.question: Can you create diagrams from an existing codebase?
questions.answer: Yes. We can analyze an existing repository, database schema, API structure, route layout, and service boundaries to produce accurate diagrams. We review the real code and architecture instead of creating generic visuals. This is useful for legacy systems, handovers, audits, refactoring, and onboarding.

questions.question: Why are architecture diagrams important for software teams?
questions.answer: Architecture diagrams improve communication, reduce onboarding time, clarify technical boundaries, and support better planning. They help teams spot dependency problems, duplicated logic, unclear ownership, and scaling risks. Good diagrams make complex systems easier to maintain and improve.

questions.question: Can diagrams help identify technical debt?
questions.answer: Yes. Architecture diagrams can reveal circular dependencies, tightly coupled modules, unclear data ownership, overloaded services, weak boundaries, and risky integration paths. They do not fix technical debt by themselves, but they make hidden structure visible so teams can plan refactoring more safely.

questions.question: Can you document Next.js, TypeScript, backend, and database architecture?
questions.answer: Yes. We can document Next.js App Router structure, React components, TypeScript modules, backend services, API routes, database schemas, Supabase tables, PostgreSQL relationships, authentication flows, and deployment architecture. The documentation can be technical enough for engineers and clear enough for stakeholders.

questions.question: How do you keep private system details secure in diagrams?
questions.answer: We avoid exposing secrets, production URLs, tokens, passwords, private keys, and sensitive credentials in diagrams. Sensitive systems can be represented with abstract labels or internal identifiers. Architecture documentation should explain structure without leaking security-critical implementation details.

questions.question: Does Devisgon provide updates after the diagrams are delivered?
questions.answer: Yes. Architecture diagrams should be updated as the system changes. Devisgon can provide update guidance, versioned diagram files, documentation maintenance, and follow-up reviews. This helps your architecture documentation stay useful instead of becoming outdated after the next development phase.
